Phenomenon

/fuh-NOM-uh-non/ — four bouncing beats: 'fuh-NOM-uh-non' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Phenomenon is something observed to happen or exist, especially when it is hard to explain.

Scientists traveled from around the world to study the strange glowing phenomenon over the desert.

Worked Example

Every November, thousands of starlings gather over the marsh at dusk and swirl into vast, shifting shapes — ribbons, spheres, waves — with no leader directing them. Researchers film it every year and still debate how each bird knows exactly where to turn.

The birds' display is a phenomenon — something clearly observed yet hard to fully explain. An ordinary 'event' is easily understood; a phenomenon draws study precisely because it resists easy explanation.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

marvel: A marvel is something that causes wonder and admiration — the feeling is the point. A phenomenon is defined by observation instead: something clearly seen to happen yet hard to explain, and a phenomenon can be studied for years without anyone finding it beautiful.

occurrence: An occurrence is anything that happens at all, from a sneeze to a storm — the most neutral label there is. A phenomenon is an occurrence that stands out: striking enough to draw serious study, and hard to fully explain even after careful observation.

wonder: A wonder is something so astonishing that people stop and stare — the word announces awe. Calling something a phenomenon says less about awe and more about study: it is observed, recorded, and puzzled over because explanation comes hard.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

commonplace: an ordinary, unremarkable thing

routine: a usual, fully expected happening

Where it sits · how much explanation it defies — event → phenomenon → miracle

event vs. phenomenon: Event is weaker than phenomenon — an event is any happening at all, while a phenomenon is striking enough to demand observation and explanation.

miracle vs. phenomenon: Miracle is stronger than phenomenon — a phenomenon is hard to explain, but a miracle seems to defy explanation entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — phen

Root — phen: to show, to appear (from Greek phainein, 'to show' — the same root spelled phan in phantom)

Suffix — -omenon

Suffix — -omenon: that which is (participle ending) (Greek)

Put it together

Put it together: Phen ('to show, to appear' — from Greek phainein) + -omenon ('that which is' — a Greek participle ending): Greek phainomenon meant 'that which appears.' A phenomenon is something that visibly shows itself to observers — even when its cause stays hidden.

Use the root in a new word: phantom

Use the root in a new word: phantom: The old sailors swore a phantom ship appeared in the fog each winter.
